passages.happening:
The Bible's first sentence is short: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (verse 1). ‘The heavens and the earth’ is a Hebrew way of saying ‘everything’, the way we might say ‘from top to bottom’.

Verse 2 describes the world before God shapes it. It is “formless and void”, in Hebrew tohu and bohu: empty, without order, not yet a place where anything can live. It is dark. There is ‘the deep’, a mass of water. And “the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.”

So the chapter opens with a problem and a presence. The problem is a world without shape and without life. The presence is God, already there, already moving over it. The rest of the chapter answers the problem: first God gives the world shape, then he fills it.
passages.hearers:
The first hearers lived among peoples who told very different stories. In Babylon's creation story, the world is made out of the body of a sea goddess, killed in battle by the god Marduk. The deep waters were a monster to be beaten.

Genesis begins with no battle at all. The deep is just water. It has no name, no will and no power to fight. Before anything else exists, God is there, and he is not one god among many. He is not born from anything, and nothing stands against him.

Ancient readers would also notice the word ‘create’, in Hebrew bara. In the Bible only God is ever said to do this. People make and build. Only God creates.

There is a question about verse 1 itself. Most Bibles read it as a complete sentence: ‘In the beginning God created’. Some Jewish scholars, and a few modern translations, read it as ‘When God began to create’, leading into verse 2. The Hebrew allows both. On the first reading, verse 1 describes the very beginning of everything.
passages.later:
The Bible returns to these opening words again and again. Psalm 33:6 says, “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made”. Jeremiah, describing his land ruined by war, says he saw the earth “formless and void” (Jeremiah 4:23), using the same two words as Genesis 1:2: judgment looks like creation run backwards. Isaiah says God “did not create it to be empty, but formed it to be inhabited” (Isaiah 45:18).

The New Testament begins its account of Jesus with the same words. John's Gospel opens, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), and says, “Through Him all things were made” (John 1:3). Hebrews says, “By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible” (Hebrews 11:3). That is the teaching the church calls creation ‘from nothing’: God did not shape the world out of something that was already there beside him.
passages.hard:
How old is the world, and how long did creation take? Genesis 1 is where that question is most often argued. Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it.

Some Christians read the days of Genesis 1 as ordinary days and hold that the earth is thousands of years old. Some take each day as a long age. Some see the days as a frame that arranges God's works. Some read them as God's workdays, like ours but not the same. Some read the week as God setting up the world as his temple. And some hold that God made living things through the long process biology describes. Each reading is held by Christians who take the Bible as God's word, and each has hard questions to answer. The site's Honest Answer ‘How should a Christian read Genesis 1?’ sets them out with care.

What all of them confess is the chapter's main claim: God made everything that exists, and nothing exists apart from him.
passages.asks: Everything starts with God, not with us. Ask what changes if the world is not an accident and not a battlefield of gods, but something made on purpose by someone good. Then ask where the formless and empty places are in your own life, and whether you believe God can still hover over them.

passages.t: Days one to three: God makes room
passages.happening:
Now God speaks. “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (verse 3). He sees that it is good, separates light from darkness, and names them day and night. Evening comes, then morning: the first day.

On the second day God makes an “expanse” to separate the waters below from the waters above, and he calls it “sky” (verses 6-8).

On the third day he gathers the waters below into seas so that dry land appears (verses 9-10). Then he tells the earth to bring forth plants: “seed-bearing plants and fruit trees, each bearing fruit with seed according to its kind” (verse 11).

Look at the pattern. In these three days God makes three spaces: light and dark, sky and sea, and dry land. He gives the formless world its shape. Each day follows the same steps: God speaks, it happens, God sees that it is good, and the day closes with evening and morning.
passages.hearers:
An ancient hearer would feel the rhythm. The same phrases come back like the lines of a song: ‘And God said’, ‘And it was so’, ‘God saw that it was good’. The chapter is written in prose, but it is built like a hymn.

They would also notice how easily things happen. In other stories the gods fight, struggle and plot. Here God only speaks, and the world obeys. There is no resistance anywhere.

The ‘expanse’ (Hebrew raqia) is the sky as it looks from the ground: a great vault overhead, with rain falling from above. Scholars debate whether ancient readers thought of it as a solid dome or simply described the sky as it appears. Either way, Genesis speaks of the world as its first hearers saw it. It is not written as a science lesson, and it does not need to be read as one.

Naming mattered too. In the ancient world, to name something was to show authority over it. God names day, night, sky, earth and seas. Darkness and the deep, which other peoples feared, are given names by God like everything else.
passages.later:
Light shining out of darkness becomes one of the Bible's great pictures of what God does for people. Paul writes, “For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The God who made the first light is the God who brings people to see who Jesus is.

The Bible's last pages answer the first day too. In the new creation “There will be no more night in the city, and they will have no need for the light of a lamp or of the sun. For the Lord God will shine on them” (Revelation 22:5).

God's speaking is also taken up in praise. Psalm 33:6 says, “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made”, and Psalm 104 walks through creation in much the same order as Genesis 1, ending in wonder: “How many are Your works, O LORD!” (Psalm 104:24).
passages.hard:
There is light on day one, but the sun does not appear until day four. How can that be? Readers noticed this long ago. In the third century the Christian teacher Origen asked how there could be days with evening and morning before the sun.

Christians have answered in different ways. Some say God made light first and the sun later, and that he does not need the sun to make light. Some say the order is not a timetable but a pattern, arranging God's works by theme. Others say the sun was there but not yet seen from the earth. These readings follow from the different ways of reading the days. Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it. What the text plainly says is that light, like everything else, comes from God's word.
passages.asks: God's first act is to bring light and order. Ask where you need God to speak light into darkness. And notice the pattern: God makes room before he fills it. Ask whether you are trying to fill a life that has never been given room.

passages.t: Days four to six: God fills what he made
passages.happening:
Now God fills the spaces he made. Day four answers day one, day five answers day two, and day six answers day three.

On the fourth day God makes lights in the sky “to distinguish between the day and the night, and let them be signs to mark the seasons and days and years” (verse 14). He makes “the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night” and the stars as well (verse 16).

On the fifth day he fills the waters and the sky: “the great sea creatures and every living thing that moves” in the water, and every bird (verse 21). He blesses them and tells them to multiply (verse 22).

On the sixth day he fills the dry land with animals: livestock, “land crawlers”, and “beasts of the earth” (verse 24). Each time, God sees that it is good. Every kind of creature is good in his eyes before human beings appear.
passages.hearers:
Notice what Genesis does not say. It does not name the sun and moon. Hebrew had ordinary words for them, but those words were also the names of gods worshiped across the region. Genesis calls them ‘the greater light’ and ‘the lesser light’. They are lamps God hung in the sky, given a job: to mark days, seasons and years. Whatever your neighbors worship, the chapter says, God made it.

The stars get only a few words: “And He made the stars as well” (verse 16). In Babylon, scholars studied the stars to read the future. Here they are an afterthought.

The “great sea creatures” of verse 21 would catch an ancient hearer's ear. The Hebrew word, tanninim, is used elsewhere for sea monsters and dragons. In other stories, such monsters fought the gods. In Genesis God simply creates them, and calls them good. And here, for the first time since verse 1, the word ‘create’ (bara) is used again.
passages.later:
Israel's law later warns against exactly what Genesis refuses to do. When you see “the sun and moon and stars”, do not “bow down and worship” them (Deuteronomy 4:19). Psalm 136 praises God who “made the great lights” and says of each one, “His loving devotion endures forever” (Psalm 136:7-9). The lights are gifts, not gods.

The sea monsters return in poetry. God “smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea” (Psalm 74:13), and Isaiah sees a day when God will “slay the dragon of the sea” (Isaiah 27:1). In those places the monster stands for chaos and evil. Genesis 1 shows that even such things are only creatures under God.

Jesus pointed to God's care for the creatures of the fifth day: “Look at the birds of the air: They do not sow or reap or gather into barns” (Matthew 6:26), yet God feeds them. The goodness of creation in Genesis 1 lies behind his words.
passages.asks: What do people today trust or fear as if it ruled their lives: the stars, the markets, the news, chance? Genesis 1 calls such things creatures, not masters. Ask what you have treated as a god that is only a light hung up to serve. And notice that God calls the animals good before people arrive. Ask how that shapes the way you treat them.

passages.t: Male and female, in God's image
passages.happening:
The sixth day slows down. Before making human beings, God speaks as if taking counsel: “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness, to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the livestock, and over all the earth itself and every creature that crawls upon it” (verse 26).

Then verse 27 breaks into poetry, and the word ‘create’ comes three times: “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.” ‘Man’ here means humankind. The verse says it straight out: male and female.

Then God blesses them and speaks to them directly, as he has spoken to no other creature: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it; rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and every creature that crawls upon the earth” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The word ‘image’ (Hebrew tselem) would have startled an ancient hearer. In their world, a king set up statues of himself in the lands he ruled to show that they belonged to him. A statue of a ruler found at Tell Fekheriye in Syria in 1979, from the 800s BC, is inscribed in Akkadian and Aramaic. Its Aramaic uses words for ‘image’ and ‘likeness’ that are related to the two words of Genesis 1:26. Kings were called the image of a god. Statues of gods stood in temples.

Genesis takes that language and gives it to every human being, not only kings. Every person is God's image in the world: his representative, showing what he is like and caring for what he made.

And the image is given to “male and female” alike. Women are not a lesser copy. Both are made in God's image, equally. Both are blessed. Both are given the task. In a world where women were often treated as property, that was a remarkable thing to say.

In Babylon's stories, humans were made as slaves, to do the gods' heavy work. In Genesis they are made as royal children, given the earth to care for.
passages.later:
The image of God is not lost when sin comes in. Genesis 5:1-2 repeats it, and Genesis 9:6 makes it the reason that murder is so grave: “for in His own image God has made mankind.” James says we cannot bless God and then curse people “who have been made in God’s likeness” (James 3:9).

Psalm 8 sings of the same dignity: “You made him ruler of the works of Your hands” (Psalm 8:6).

The New Testament calls Jesus himself “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). He is the true human being, the one who shows perfectly what God is like. And it speaks of believers as having “put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (Colossians 3:10). Paul also writes, “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).
passages.hard:
Who is ‘Us’ in “Let Us make man”? Readers have answered in three main ways. Some think God is speaking to his heavenly court, the angels around his throne, though he alone does the creating (verse 27 says ‘God created’). Some think it is a ‘plural of majesty’, the way a king might say ‘we’. Christians have long heard in it a hint of what the New Testament makes plain, that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Many think the first hearers could not yet have heard that, and that the hint is seen clearly only looking back. These readings can be held together, and these notes do not choose between them.

What does ‘rule’ and ‘subdue’ mean? Not a licence to destroy. The rule given here is modeled on God's own rule in the chapter: he orders, blesses, feeds and calls things good. Israel's law later forbids ruling over a person ‘harshly’ (Leviticus 25:43). Christians differ on how to apply this to care for the earth today, but no reading of Genesis makes human rule a right to ruin what God called good.
passages.asks: Every person you will meet today bears God's image: the stranger, the enemy, the person who annoys you, and you yourself. Ask what changes if you believe that. Ask whether you treat women and men as equal bearers of that image. And ask how you are ruling the small part of the world given to you: like God, who blesses, or like a tyrant, who takes.

passages.happening:
God now gives food. “Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant on the face of all the earth, and every tree whose fruit contains seed. They will be yours for food” (verse 29). He gives every green plant to the animals and birds as well (verse 30).

Then comes the verdict. “And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good” (verse 31). Six times the chapter has said ‘good’. Now, with the whole world finished and human beings in it, it says ‘very good’.

The sixth day ends. But the week is not finished. The seventh day, the day of rest, follows in Genesis 2:1-3. The chapter break was added much later and cuts the story in the middle.
passages.hearers:
In Babylon's stories, people were made to feed the gods. Temples set out meals for the gods every day. Genesis turns this upside down. Here God feeds people, and the animals too. He needs nothing from them. He gives.

The first food in Genesis is plants, for people and animals alike. Only after the flood does God give people permission to eat meat (Genesis 9:3). Readers have seen in this a picture of a world at peace, without killing.

‘Very good’ would also speak to people who had known suffering. The world as God made it is not evil, and the body is not a prison. Matter, food, animals, men and women: all of it is good. Whatever has gone wrong since, the fault does not lie in the way God made things.
passages.later:
The Bible's hope for the future reaches back to this verse. Isaiah sees a time when animals will no longer kill. Paul says that creation now “was subjected to futility” but waits “in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay” (Romans 8:20-21). The world is no longer as ‘very good’ as it was made, but God has not given up on it.

The Bible's last vision is not an escape from this world but its renewal: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21:1). The God who called his world very good intends to make it so again.
passages.asks: God gives before he asks anything. Ask whether you see your food, your body and the world around you as gifts from a generous God. And when you are tempted to think the physical world, or your own body, is less spiritual than your soul, remember what God called it: very good.
